A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TwinVLA and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Retained experiments and method components can be matched reliably across revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original real-world robot experiments, TwinVLA simulation evaluations, ablations, and SingleVLA results on LIBERO.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds real-world manipulation, language-following, and robustness evaluations.

M1.justification: Both versions use selective VLM duplication, shared vision and action modules, joint attention, MoE processing of shared tokens, and attention re-weighting. The new MoE equation and expanded pseudocode document existing components; they do not establish a changed algorithm. The omitted language head is newly disclosed rather than demonstrated to be newly removed.

E1.justification: Real-world coverage expands from three manipulation tasks to five, adding Fold towel and Extract hexkey, plus a real-world Put X into pot language-following task set. Low-light and distractor conditions add physical-world test scenarios. The OXE composition, LIBERO coverage, Tabletop-Sim tasks, and RoboTwin tasks remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain DP, RDT-1B, and π0, with RDT-1B and π0 used for language following. The LIBERO comparator sets also remain unchanged. Newly discussed methods such as Anybimanual are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: The training table changes stated precision from mixed FP32/BF16 in v1 Table 2 to BF16 in v2 Table 3; this does not establish that experiments were rerun. New robustness testing applies lighting and distractor perturbations. Existing training budgets and standard rollout counts remain unchanged; the explicit action-chunk length is additional disclosure.

E4.justification: v2 adds real-world robustness tests under low light and distractors, where v1's robustness evaluation was confined to simulation. It also extends component ablations to the expanded real-world task collection and adds failure case studies for towel folding and hexkey extraction in Appendix D. The simulation and LIBERO ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same statement about identical random seeds for LIBERO evaluation. Neither adds repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial real-world results, including TwinVLA success rates of 90% for Fold towel and 80% for Extract hexkey. New real-world language-following scores are 51.8% for TwinVLA, 33.3% for RDT-1B, and 62.9% for π0. Existing appendix entries also change: TwinVLA's Close bag score falls from 0.65 to 0.60 and Entirely off from 0.55 to 0.45. Real-world aggregates and ablations cover an expanded task mix, so their changes are not same-setting gains. LIBERO and simulation table values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 removes the explicit Gaussian interpolation path, timestep distribution, and reference-flow definition, retaining the generic flow-matching loss and Euler update. These mathematical specifications are not relocated to the appendices. The added MoE equation formalizes an already described mechanism; no theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same central claims: composing pretrained single-arm policies enables efficient bimanual adaptation without bimanual pretraining, outperforming RDT-1B and approaching π0. The revised introduction and conclusion emphasize the existing adaptation argument without materially changing its scope.

C2.justification: Section 6 replaces the explicit limitation about forgetting single-arm skills after fine-tuning with limited generalization attributed to the visual distribution shift from two arms. No evidence establishes that forgetting was resolved. v2 also adds qualifications about distractor sensitivity, interpretations of failures in tightly coordinated tasks, and a rationale linking absolute EEF actions to reduced error accumulation.

D1.justification: v2 adds integrated pseudocode, explicit linear-softmax routing and output-averaging operations, the 20-step action chunk, robot-base coordinate frame, and the explanation for SingleVLA's 0.8B size. Appendix E replaces a future release promise with stated Tabletop-Sim code availability and a repository link. However, explicit flow-matching sampling and target details are removed. These are documentation changes, not evidence of new implementations or externally verified availability.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from a broad VLA overview toward prior bimanual coordination architectures, adding discussion of Anybimanual, InterACT, Bi-VLA methods, and PerAct-related work. TwinVLA is now explicitly positioned against specialized coordination architectures as well as monolithic models, emphasizing compatibility with generalist VLAs.

P1.justification: Section 2 is substantially rewritten, flow-matching exposition is condensed, and a new mixture-architecture subsection precedes an expanded algorithm-centered method presentation. Robustness and language-following subsections exchange order, Appendix C is reorganized, and terminology, limitations, and introductory framing receive substantial editing.

P2.justification: Figure 2 changes dataset-size axes from episodes to hours. Real-world setup, performance, language-following, initial-distribution, and qualitative figures gain panels or categories. v2 adds a robustness table and scene figure, expands the subtask and hyperparameter tables, and introduces additional algorithm displays. These are substantive display changes beyond renumbering and pagination.

improvement.justification: The expanded physical-robot tests strengthen evidence about coordination and real-world generalization, while clearer pseudocode and corrected table entries improve assessability. The gain is limited by reporting problems: Section 5.6 claims superiority over both baselines despite Figure 8a showing real-world language-following performance below π0, 51.8% versus 62.9%. Removing explicit flow-matching details and the single-arm-forgetting caveat also reduces completeness. On balance, the additional evidence supports a limited overall improvement.
